concepts.def: Gap between neurones crossed by chemicals.
Detect stimuli and carry out responses.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Grey Matter — a core area of A-Level Biology.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Grey Matter brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Grey Matter.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Cone cells in the retina are responsible for:
options: colour vision in bright light
monochrome vision in dim light
detecting sound vibrations
secreting tears

mcqs.q: An action potential is generated only when the membrane reaches:
options: threshold potential
resting potential
the refractory period
equilibrium potential

mcqs.q: At a synapse, the signal is passed to the next neurone by:
options: a neurotransmitter diffusing across the gap
an electrical spark jumping the gap
the two membranes fusing together
an enzyme cutting the axon

mcqs.q: Rod cells give high sensitivity in dim light because:
options: many rods converge on one neurone, allowing summation
each rod has its own neurone for sharp detail
they contain three colour pigments
they are found only in the fovea

mcqs.q: Why can't you see colour well in dim light?
options: The two neurones are fused so the current flows continuously.
Colours physically disappear from objects at night.
Dim light damages the cones so colour vision is lost.
Rod cells, which work in dim light, are not colour-sensitive; cone cells give colour but need bright light to respond.

mcqs.q: Does a stronger stimulus produce a larger action potential?
options: A stronger stimulus produces a larger action potential.
The two neurones are fused so the current flows continuously.
No - action potentials are all-or-nothing; a stronger stimulus increases their frequency, not their size.
A stronger stimulus makes the action potential travel backwards.

mcqs.q: How is a signal passed across a synapse?
options: The electrical impulse jumps straight across the synaptic gap.
The two neurones are fused so the current flows continuously.
A neurotransmitter is released, diffuses across the gap and binds receptors on the next neurone, so transmission here is chemical.
Dim light damages the cones so colour vision is lost.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Brain plasticity”?
options: A specialised nerve cell that conducts electrical impulses, consisting of dendrites, a cell body and an axon often insulated by a myelin sheath.
The ability of the brain to change its structure and neural connections in response to experience, learning or damage.
A rapid reversal of membrane potential, depolarising to about +40 mV, that travels along an axon once a threshold stimulus is reached.
Retinal cells that function in bright light, allow colour vision through three types and give high visual acuity at the fovea.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Cone cells”?
options: A specialised nerve cell that conducts electrical impulses, consisting of dendrites, a cell body and an axon often insulated by a myelin sheath.
A junction between two neurones where a neurotransmitter is released, diffuses across the gap and stimulates receptors on the next cell.
Retinal cells that function in bright light, allow colour vision through three types and give high visual acuity at the fovea.
Light-sensitive cells in the retina that work in dim light, give monochrome vision and show high sensitivity but low visual acuity.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Neurone”?
options: The ability of the brain to change its structure and neural connections in response to experience, learning or damage.
Light-sensitive cells in the retina that work in dim light, give monochrome vision and show high sensitivity but low visual acuity.
A junction between two neurones where a neurotransmitter is released, diffuses across the gap and stimulates receptors on the next cell.
A specialised nerve cell that conducts electrical impulses, consisting of dendrites, a cell body and an axon often insulated by a myelin sheath.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Synapse”?
options: Retinal cells that function in bright light, allow colour vision through three types and give high visual acuity at the fovea.
A junction between two neurones where a neurotransmitter is released, diffuses across the gap and stimulates receptors on the next cell.
Light-sensitive cells in the retina that work in dim light, give monochrome vision and show high sensitivity but low visual acuity.
The ability of the brain to change its structure and neural connections in response to experience, learning or damage.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Rod cells”?
options: Retinal cells that function in bright light, allow colour vision through three types and give high visual acuity at the fovea.
Light-sensitive cells in the retina that work in dim light, give monochrome vision and show high sensitivity but low visual acuity.
The ability of the brain to change its structure and neural connections in response to experience, learning or damage.
A specialised nerve cell that conducts electrical impulses, consisting of dendrites, a cell body and an axon often insulated by a myelin sheath.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Action potential”?
options: A junction between two neurones where a neurotransmitter is released, diffuses across the gap and stimulates receptors on the next cell.
Light-sensitive cells in the retina that work in dim light, give monochrome vision and show high sensitivity but low visual acuity.
The ability of the brain to change its structure and neural connections in response to experience, learning or damage.
A rapid reversal of membrane potential, depolarising to about +40 mV, that travels along an axon once a threshold stimulus is reached.

mcqs.q: Approximately what peak membrane potential (in mV) is reached during an action potential?
options: 40 mV
70 mV
-70 mV
0 mV

free_texts.q: Type the key term that means: "Large molecule formed from many monomers joined by condensation reactions."
free_texts.hint: It's one of the six key terms above.

sequence.def: Inside -70 mV; Na+/K+ pump maintains the gradient
Stimulus depolarises membrane to about -55 mV
Na+ channels open; inside becomes +40 mV
Na+ channels close, K+ channels open; inside falls
K+ overshoot drops potential below -70 mV
Na+/K+ pump restores the -70 mV resting potential
